entries.title: Federal judge told 'things are no longer quiet' as Midway Blitz lawsuit faces critical November ruling
entries.summary: <p>The judge who once challenged<b> </b>Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino<b> </b>and tried to limit the feds’ use of force<b> </b>during Operation Midway Blitz<b> </b>is now expected to decide in mid-November whether she’ll allow <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/12/illinois-chicago-sue-trump-administration-over-organized-bombardment-under-noem-bovino" target="_blank" >Illinois and Chicago’s<b> </b>lawsuit</a> over the deportation campaign<b> </b>to move forward.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis<b> </b>said she will rule Nov. 17 on Homeland Security’s<b> </b>bid to have the lawsuit tossed out. She set the ruling date after listening to three-and-a-half hours<b> </b>of arguments Wednesday in the same courtroom where she once <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/24/federal-judge-orders-border-patrol-commander-greg-bovino-into-her-courtroom" target="_blank" >ordered Bovino to appear</a>. </p><p>The arguments came with Chicago on the cusp of marking the one-year anniversary of Midway Blitz. It began Sept. 8, 2025,<b> </b>and led to eight weeks of chaos, tear gas and fear. The feds say the campaign<b> </b>ended<b> </b>late in 2025, but Illinois’ lawyers clearly aren’t convinced.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/12/illinois-chicago-sue-trump-administration-over-organized-bombardment-under-noem-bovino" >Trump administration hit with federal lawsuit over ‘occupation of Illinois and Chicago’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>In fact, attorneys recently<b> </b>accused the feds of resuming<b> </b>their use of chemical munitions, warrantless arrests and enforcement activity near sensitive locations like courthouses. Chicago’s immigration court<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/24/chaotic-crowded-chicago-immigration-mega-court-hearings-are-fueling-record-deportation-orders" target="_blank" >led the country<b> </b>in hearings</a><b> </b>in June.</p><p>“Things are no longer quiet,” Illinois attorney Vikas<b> </b>Didwania<b> </b>told Ellis in a court filing last week.</p><p>The lawsuit alleges the Trump administration “unleashed an organized bombardment on the State of Illinois and the City of Chicago”<b> </b>designed to “coerce”<b> </b>them<b> </b>into abandoning sanctuary policies, which mean local authorities won’t help track down immigrants without legal status.</p><p>Among other things, it asks Ellis to block similar future attempts at immigration enforcement by Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" >Judge blasts Trump’s Chicago border ‘Blitz,’ extends curbs on use of force that ‘shocks the conscience’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Ellis, appointed to the bench by then-President Barack Obama in 2013, took over the case after handling similar litigation last fall. She’d <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >entered a preliminary injunction</a><b> </b>Nov. 6<b> </b>that limited the feds’ use of force<b> </b>during the campaign, reading<b> </b>Carl Sandburg’s<b> </b>“Chicago”<b> </b>poem<b> </b>as she ruled.</p><p>The 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals blocked<b> </b>and later vacated her order.</p><p>Wednesday’s hearing in the new case largely turned on technical legal arguments, including whether Illinois and Chicago have the right to sue. But Ellis and the lawyers explored the differences between the 2025 campaign and the aggressive, albeit quieter, immigration enforcement that’s now ongoing.</p><p>The judge also reflected on an effort to enforce one of her orders last fall.</p><p>Ellis brought it up while asking the lawyers to identify the line between legitimate immigration enforcement and the kind of coercion alleged by Illinois and Chicago. She wanted to know, “at what point do I … step out of my lane?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino walks out of the Dirksen Federal Courthouse after testifying during a hearing about immigration enforcement in Chicago, Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. | Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Before she handed down her injunction last fall, Ellis had entered a similar temporary restraining order. Then, in late October, she ordered Bovino<b> </b>to appear in her courtroom<b> </b>to discuss whether that order was being followed. The former Border Patrol official, who became the public face of Midway Blitz, has since retired.</p><p>“I had issued a valid order saying, ‘this is what can be used, this is the amount of force that is appropriate in this particular setting,’” Ellis said Wednesday, “and it was certainly my impression that that order was not being followed, right?”</p><p>The judge then tried to force Bovino to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/28/border-patrol-gregory-bovino-federal-court" target="_blank" >return to her courtroom</a> regularly, over the course of a week. She explained Wednesday that she’d wanted to “look backwards”<b> </b>with him on events that had already transpired. Had she asked him to tell her what he was doing the next day, she said, that would have amounted to her improperly “managing”<b> </b>the executive branch.</p><p>But there wound up being “a difference of opinion on whether that violated the separation of powers”<b> </b>between the courts and the executive branch, she said.</p><p>The federal appeals court<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/31/bovinos-daily-meetings-with-judge-would-infringe-on-separation-of-powers-appeals-court-says" target="_blank" >ruled that it did</a>.</p><p>“I think that it is very illustrative of how tricky that can be,” Ellis told the lawyers Wednesday.</p><p>Justice Department<b> </b>attorney Brantley<b> </b>Mayers<b> </b>argued that Illinois and Chicago want to have it both ways: They don’t want to support the federal government’s immigration efforts, and they don’t want the feds to be allowed to deploy more resources to do it on its own.</p><p>But Ellis told him, “I don’t think that’s what they’re arguing, at all.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/05/crucial-hearing-over-feds-use-of-force-could-reveal-incredible-bovino-testimony-wednesday" >‘It’s a disgrace': Chicagoans describe jarring encounters with feds as judge prepares to rule on ‘blitz’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“What they are complaining about, at this point, is that there were a number of warrantless arrests,” Ellis said. “That people were being stopped on the street. That people were being stopped dropping off their kids to school. That people were being stopped going to church. Going to the grocery store. That people living in an apartment complex had agents in the middle of the night rappelling down the side of their building and coming in.</p><p>“That that sort of behavior, combined with the treatment of people who were protesting the increased enforcement … that that crossed the line from enforcement to coercion.”</p><p>Lee Reeves, Mayers’ co-counsel, told the judge the lawsuit was brought by the wrong claimants making the wrong claims. He said individuals who claim to have been harmed during the campaign should be pursuing lawsuits or criminal charges, instead.</p><p>Several individuals have done exactly that. And many have called for federal agents to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/jon-seidel?p=00000198-1631-d49b-af99-df3def400000.2" target="_blank" >face criminal charges</a> for alleged wrongdoing during Midway Blitz.</p><p>Meanwhile, Illinois attorney Paul<b> </b>Berks invited the feds to make another claim: That the lawsuit is “moot.” In other words, there’s no reason to worry about Midway Blitz happening again.</p><p>Reeves and<b> </b>Mayers<b> </b>did not take him up on the offer.</p><p>“We would love to see the evidence that it’s not going to happen again,” Berks said.</p>
entries.author: Jon Seidel

entries.title: Even on night bats bash Jacob Misiorowski, eyes on bullpen as Jacob Webb takes liner off arm in Cubs loss
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> can’t shake <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/02/cubs-bullpen-relief-pitchers-stats-daniel-palencia-jacob-webb-trent-thornton-justin-steele-javier-assad-edward-cabrera-pedro-ramirez" >their bullpen blues</a>.</p><p>Even on a night the Cubs’ bats did the unthinkable and scorched Cy Young favorite <b>Jacob Misiorowski</b> for five runs – the Brewers’ fireballing ace hadn’t given up more than three earned runs in a start this season – the story was what the team’s pitching staff couldn’t do in a 9-5 loss: keep their division-leading rivals at bay.</p><p>Lefty starter <b>David Peterson</b> was the main culprit, coughing up a 5-3 lead and getting tagged for six runs without getting out of the fourth inning.</p><p>But a relief corps that’s struggled lately grabbed negative headlines again, with righty closer <b>Jacob Webb</b> knocked out of the game in the top of the ninth inning after taking a line-drive comebacker off his right forearm.</p><p>Manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> updated after the game that X-rays were negative.</p><p>Though he’s been the team’s top reliever this season, Webb – who was charged with a couple runs after departing Wednesday – has contributed the loudest moments of a sour stretch for the bullpen, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/26/cubs-walk-off-loss-diamondbacks-clay-holmes-kevin-gausman-daniel-palencia-jacob-webb-bullpen" >surrendering walk-off homers in consecutive appearances</a> on the Cubs’ most recent road trip.</p><p>But he hasn’t been alone, with righty <b>Trent Thornton</b> tagged for six runs in two outings against the Reds last weekend and <b>Daniel Palencia</b> balking a runner home and allowing a game-flipping homer in Tuesday’s loss.</p><p>Palencia gave up a run Wednesday, too, and he’s got a 14.54 ERA in five outings since returning from the IL.</p><p>“We need Daniel. The results have not been good,” Counsell said after the game. “The best thing we can do is get him out there as much as we can.</p><p>“We need our bullpen guys to get outs, and Daniel’s one of the key guys we need to get going. We’re going to keep putting him out there.”</p><p>There will be more to come on Webb’s status, but any missed time would be a big problem for the Cubs as they look to right their relief ship in time to count on their bullpen arms in the postseason.</p><p>“Hopefully he can get back soon,” third baseman <b>Alex Bregman</b> said.</p><p><b>Making a mess of ‘The Miz’</b></p><p>He’s “The Miz” and nobody beats him?</p><p>Most days. But not Wednesday.</p><p>The Cubs struck early, with Bregman smacking a two-run, first-inning homer. Outfielder <b>Tyrone Taylor</b>’s RBI single and a Bregman two-out, two-run base hit added three runs in the second.</p><p>Though the Cubs started the day with baseball’s highest scoring offense, they’d faced Misiorowski twice previously this summer and managed only one run against him in 12 innings.</p><p>This time, they chased him from the game after four innings, matching his shortest start of the campaign.</p><p>“It was a pass-the-line night against Misiorowski,” Counsell said, “and that’s a pretty darn good job.”</p><p>They weren’t as successful against the Brewers’ bullpen, though, mustering only two hits after the second inning, and the Cubs fell to nine games back in the NL Central standings.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Police warn of strong-arm robberies and thefts on Northwest Side
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are alerting the public to recent strong-arm robberies and thefts from vehicles in the Portage Park and Irving Park neighborhoods.</p><p>Police believe the alleged thieves, which were reported from late July through Wednesday morning.<br>targeted people at banks and gas stations, typically during daytime hours, according to an alert.</p><p>In some instances, police said the assailants have entered occupied vehicles and taken items. During some thefts, the alleged perpetrators wait until the car is empty, steal money or other items, and flee to a car waiting nearby. </p><p>Police said during these robberies, the alleged offenders have not spoken to the victims or displayed weapons.</p><p>The thefts reported so far include the following locations: <br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-dc9f1f32-a73f-11f1-8dbf-9bb0082d645b"><li>6400 block of West Irving Park Road on July 23 at 1:05 p.m. </li><li>3200 block of West Irving Park Road on July 27 at 12:23 p.m. </li><li>4400 block of North Central Avenue on Aug. 5 at 12:43 p.m. </li><li>3200 block of West Irving Park Road on Aug. 11 at 10:48 a.m. </li><li>5200 block of North Cicero Avenue on Aug. 16 at 5:05 p.m. </li><li>3900 block of North Kilpatrick Avenue on Aug. 18 at 10:57 a.m. </li><li>4600 block of West Irving Park Road on Aug. 31 at 1:30 p.m. </li><li>5600 block of West Montrose Avenue on Sept. 2 at 11:43 a.m. </li></ul><p>Police described the suspects as two men dressed in black and wearing black face masks.</p><p>The vehicles being used by the alleged assailants include a black Nissan Rogue, a black Lincoln SUV, and a black Porsche Macan, police said.</p><p>Residents are encouraged to be aware of their surroundings and report any suspicious activity immediately, police said.</p><p>Anyone with information is encouraged to contact Area 5 detectives at 312-746-7394 or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com and provide reference number P26-5-014.</p>

entries.title: Hersh’s Fridge dedicated in Skokie in memory of Hersh Goldberg-Polin
entries.summary: <p>A kosher community fridge honoring Hersh Goldberg-Polin, a 23-year-old with Chicago ties who was taken hostage and later killed by Hamas, was dedicated Wednesday in Skokie.</p><p>Hersh’s Fridge, which organizers describe as the country’s first kosher community fridge, is open 24 hours a day and offers prepared meals, produce, groceries and dry goods to anyone who needs them.</p><p>The project grew from the work of Solu, an Orthodox Jewish bridge-building initiative, executive director Rabbi Hody Nemes said.</p><p>Nemes said the community drew inspiration from community fridges in Chicago and Evanston.</p><p>Solu volunteers had also stocked non-kosher fridges and had wondered about creating a kosher fridge serving the Jewish community and its neighbors, he said.</p><p>For several years, the idea seemed like a “pipe dream,” Nemes said.</p><p>Goldberg-Polin was taken hostage in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack in Israel. A group met Sept. 1, 2024 — the day after learning Goldberg-Polin’s body had been found in a tunnel in Gaza — to consider whether the kosher fridge idea was feasible.</p><p>When the group watched a livestream of Goldberg-Polin’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/israel-hamas-war/2024/09/22/american-hostage-hersh-goldberg-polin-israel-hamas-gaza-oct7-memorial-skokie" target="_blank" >funeral</a>, they heard his parents say, “May his memory be a revolution,” Nemes said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> 8825 East Prairie Rd.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The group wanted to honor that as a call for kindness and bringing people together, he said.</p><p>“We want to be part of that revolution,” Nemes said.</p><p>Goldberg-Polin’s parents, Chicago natives Rachel Goldberg and Jon Polin, gave the group permission to use their son’s name and have become increasingly involved with the project since, said Leah Rubin, Solu’s vice president and co-chair of Hersh’s Fridge.</p><p>The fridge launched in pilot form last October and will remain a permanent resource in Skokie, she said.</p><p>Rubin said the project was created to both address food insecurity and food waste.</p><p>Rising food costs, economic insecurity and cuts to benefits have contributed to growing need in the area, she said.</p><p>Access to the fridge is intentionally anonymous, allowing anyone from any background to use it, Rubin said.</p><p>Organizers estimate it has been accessed about 50 times a day so far, though that number is difficult to track when including anonymous parties who bring in donations while collecting other food items, Nemes said.</p><p>One refrigerator holds certified kosher meals from at least six area restaurants and caterers. A second holds packaged and labeled food prepared in kosher homes, Rubin said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Torrence Avenue Bridge reopens after being stuck due to heat-related issue
entries.summary: <p>Commuters faced headaches in multiple directions Wednesday as the Torrence Avenue Bridge got stuck in the raised position late Wednesday afternoon, just hours after the DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge reopened following a similar occurrence.</p><p>The bridge — located over the Calumet River — was stuck for more than an hour, starting at 4:30 p.m., according to Erica Schroeder, director of public affairs for the Chicago Department of Transportation.</p><p>Schroeder confirmed the issue with the Torrence Avenue bridge this afternoon was heat-related.</p><p>"Thermal expansion caused by the high temperatures affected the bridge’s operation," Schroeder explained.</p><p>CDOT crews responded to the scene and returned the bridge to its normal operating position, Schroeder said. The bridge reopened to traffic shortly after 5:30 p.m., she said.</p><p>The city’s Office of Emergency Management and Communications <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/ChicagoOEMC/status/2095290854676038104?s=20" target="_blank" ><u>confirmed</u></a> via social media at 6:20 p.m. that the Torrence Avenue Bridge had been “stuck in the up position” and said hot weather caused the issue. The office urged drivers to use alternate routes.</p><p>The DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge had become <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/02/lake-shore-drive-bridge-river" target="_blank" ><u>stuck open</u></a> during a routine lift around 10 a.m., leaving it off-limits to drivers for more than four hours before returning to its original position. </p><p>A Chicago Fire Department boat could be seen spraying water on the structure, apparently to cool it down. Chicago was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/01/september-october-chicago-heat-wave-is-this-normal" target="_blank" >under a heat advisory</a> Wednesday. The temperature had reached 90 degrees by early afternoon.</p>

entries.title: Another Chicago bridge gets stuck in sweltering heat hours after DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge reopens
entries.summary: <p>Commuters faced headaches in multiple directions Wednesday as the Torrence Avenue Bridge got stuck in the raised position late Wednesday afternoon, just hours after the DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge reopened following a similar occurrence.</p><p>The city’s Office of Emergency Management and Communications <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/ChicagoOEMC/status/2095290854676038104?s=20" target="_blank" ><u>confirmed</u></a> via social media at 6:20 p.m. that the Torrence Avenue Bridge — located over the Calumet River on Far South Side — was “stuck in the up position” and said hot weather caused the issue. The office urged drivers to use alternate routes.</p><p>The bridge — located over the Calumet River — was stuck for more than an hour, starting at 4:30 p.m., according to Erica Schroeder, director of public affairs for the Chicago Department of Transportation.</p><p>Schroeder confirmed the issue with the Torrence Avenue bridge was heat-related.</p><p>"Thermal expansion caused by the high temperatures affected the bridge’s operation," Schroeder explained.</p><p>CDOT crews responded to the scene and returned the bridge to its normal operating position, Schroeder said. The bridge was reopened to traffic by 5:30 p.m.</p><p>Just hours earlier, the DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge was reopened to traffic Wednesday afternoon, over four hours after the bridge became stuck open during a routine lift.</p><p>With the bridge unable to close all the way, traffic was snarled up and down the drive.</p><p>The bridge over the Chicago River "experienced a heat-related issue preventing it from fully closing" around 10 a.m. after it was lifted for a large yacht to pass beneath, according to the Chicago Department of Transportation.</p><p>Crews then spent the next several hours trying to get the bridge to close completely. A Chicago Fire Department boat could be seen spraying water on the structure, apparently to cool it down. Chicago was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/01/september-october-chicago-heat-wave-is-this-normal" target="_blank" >under a heat advisory</a> Wednesday. entries.title: In return from injured list, Davis Martin looked like the starting pitcher the White Sox need
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON – The biggest potential advantage for the Cleveland Guardians as they chase the White Sox in the American League Central standings is starting pitching.</p><p>With their pitching development engine, the Guardians once more have a deep rotation led by All-Star rookie Parker Messick. The White Sox’ top <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/18/white-sox-noah-schultz-hagen-smith-tanner-mcdougal-david-sandlin-brian-bannister-will-venable-erick-fedde-jose-urquidy-davis-martin-al-central" target="_blank" ><u>pitching prospects have been getting a lesson in how development isn’t linear</u></a>, and the club has spent the summer piecing their rotation together with bullpen games and openers.</p><p>Opening day starter Shane Smith is working in relief now. Of their four-best pitching prospects, only Hagen Smith is in the majors and is also in the bullpen. The biggest potential source of stability for the Sox rotation down the stretch was just activated off the injured list in Davis Martin, who issued a reminder of such with 5 2/3 scoreless innings Wednesday night against the Astros.</p><p>The best argument in favor of Martin’s ability to suddenly become a rotation anchor in the final month is that he’s done it before–this season. Even the yeoman back-end starter version of Martin from years past would be a boost for the Sox. But as he carried a 2.00 ERA and 27% strikeout rate through Memorial Day this year, Martin looked bound for an All-Star appearance and like someone who could start a playoff game.</p><p>“He was really suppressing damage,” said Sox senior advisor to pitching Brian Bannister. “I think it's his ability to diversify his pitches to hit different parts of the zone with different shapes.”</p><p>At his best, the 29-year-old right-hander’s command of a six-pitch mix lends him an improvisational style. In an age of hyper-intentional gameplanning, Martin is the rare starter who is really out there reading swings and pitching with guile to lift his results above his pure stuff.</p><p>Even as his performance wavered, and he entered Wednesday night with a 7.06 ERA since June 1, the White Sox have expressed confidence they have the video and biomechanical information to return Martin to his baselines.</p><p>“With him and with all the guys, we know what good looks like,” said pitching coach Zach Bove.</p><p>Almost every pitcher has some weaknesses baked into their strengths, and Martin is no different. The arm action that gives him great feel for spinning breaking balls and even enables his wonky kick-changeup, also asks a lot from his body over the long haul.</p><p>“He kind of drops his arm down and it's a very arm-heavy delivery, so there's definitely an element of fatigue,” Bannister told the Sun-Times. “You see that in just the velocities.”</p><p>Per FanGraphs, Martin averaged 94.2 mph on his four-seam fastball through May, and 93.6 mph since. That’s a real dip, but also small enough for Martin and the Sox to focus more on command. When he slouches in his posture on the mound, his arm will dip alongside it and suddenly his six-pitch mix shrinks to trying to groove fastballs to get back in the count. When he began overcorrecting to the point of leaning backwards, it was no good either.</p><p>“Just one little change, and then it just keeps snowballing,” Martin said. “You just think everything's going fine, and then all of a sudden you're just out of luck. Over the course of 162 games, that happens.”</p><p>Fittingly, the Sox seized upon Martin developing a middle finger blister just as his results reached their nadir as an opportunity for both a rest and reset. He only had a single five-inning Triple-A rehab outing, but the club saw proof of concept.</p><p>“The delivery stuff that he had been working on when he was on IL, it showed out,” said Bove.</p><p>In striking out three and walking just one on Wednesday, touching 96 mph, and cutting through the heart of the Houston batting order to wriggle out of a third-inning jam that saw runners at the corners with no one out, Martin furthered his case that he can be the starter the Sox need.</p>

entries.title: Chicago extends program offering free Wifi to CPS students
entries.summary: <p>More than 28,000 Chicago Public Schools students will have access to free internet at home this year thanks to the extension of the Chicago Connected program.</p><p>The program launched in 2020 in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and a shift to remote learning. Since then, more than 60,000 students have gained access to reliable home internet to complete homework and access online resources, the city of Chicago said in a news release.</p><p>“Making sure that our young people and families have access to Wifi, the internet, it's a critical component of their development,” Mayor Brandon Johnson told the Sun-Times. “As a former public school teacher, I know how important it is for students to have access to the world, to the internet.”</p><p>About $2 million was dedicated to the effort, with much of the up-front costs covered by the continuation of service from prior years, according to a city spokesman. </p><p>The Department of Technology and Innovation saved money by moving IT services to the cloud and other cost-saving measures, meaning the cost of the program could be funded by CPS and the city instead of through partnerships with internet providers and community organizations.</p><p>Around 93% of the program’s families were categorized as economically disadvantaged, and almost all of the 20 community areas with the largest improvement in connectivity rates are on the South and West Sides of the city.</p><p>“That economic disadvantage did not go away with the pandemic; the pandemic exposed what many of us have always known, that the world is cut off from families who are historically left out,” Johnson said.</p><p>Families also noted internet access benefitted them beyond schooling, helping with email communication and searching for information online, according to the news release. Johnson said he’s heard from families who are also able to stay in contact with family members when they’re away from the home, like a student whose marching band practices can go late into the evening.</p><p>“It becomes, really, a safety mechanism, where they're able to monitor the whereabouts of their loved ones,” Johnson said. “It's those kinds of elements that I think people sometimes take for granted.”</p>

entries.title: Cubs need to lose bullpen blues to be best version of themselves come October: ‘These are guys we count on’
entries.summary: <p>In a 162-game season, bullpen pitchers are going to have bad stretches.</p><p>Sometimes, those stretches are going to overlap.</p><p>There’s nothing terribly abnormal about what the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> are experiencing right now, a string of bad days for the relief corps.</p><p>But it’s the time of year when the lights are getting bright. A bullpen that has been generally effective throughout much of the summer is having a rough go at a bad time.</p><p>In the span of 11 games, righty closer <b>Jacob Webb</b> coughed up walk-off home runs in consecutive outings, righty <b>Trent Thornton</b> was rocked for six runs and three homers in a pair of appearances against the Reds, and righty fireballer <b>Daniel Palencia</b> gave up the lead to the Brewers, balking a run home and serving up a game-flipping homer — though he was one of four relievers to combine to allow six runs in that loss.</p><p>Not great.</p><p>Though there are several notable pitchers either rehabbing from injury or stashed in the minor leagues — righties <b>Edward Cabrera</b>, <b>Shelby Miller</b> and <b>Javier Assad</b>, plus lefty <b>Justin Steele</b> — it’s unknown how likely it is that those guys, aside from Assad, make significant contributions to the relief unit.</p><p>Instead of waiting for saviors, the Cubs are focused on steadying this group before the season’s most important games.</p><p>“You try to figure out: How are we going to be our best team? And it’s with these guys pitching well,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Wednesday. “These are the guys we need to pitch well. The way to do that is to get them back out there and have them pitch again.</p><p>“You get beat. And it’s no fun, and it stinks. But if you’re not confident, that’s how you get your confidence back. If you’re struggling with something, that’s how you find it. You find it out there on the field, when the competition’s going on and the other side’s trying to get you.</p><p>“These are guys we count on, and we need them. And the best way for us to be the best team is to get them back out there.”</p><p>These games, though, are important, too.</p><p>These bullpen blues could be a passing bummer. But any lingering problems could prove exceptionally costly down the stretch and into the playoffs.</p><h3><b>Justin time?</b></h3><p>Steele made his long-awaited return to game action Wednesday, making a minor league rehab appearance with Triple-A Iowa.</p><p>Steele has been out since April of last season, recovering from elbow surgery and a setback earlier this year.</p><p>He faced 10 batters Wednesday, retiring five of them and allowing three runs, only one earned, on four hits.</p><p>Though Steele is hopeful this is the next step in a return to the major league mound this season, Cubs brass has cautioned against assuming the southpaw will be able to pitch out of the team’s bullpen before the campaign’s end.</p><p>“I’m excited for him that he’s getting back out there,” team president <b>Jed Hoyer</b> said Tuesday. “As it relates to this team, we’ll see. We’re not in development mode at this point.</p><p>“If he can come back and he can help us, he’s going to come back and he’s going to help us. If there’s rust and he needs more time, it’s not the time to do that.</p><p>“I’m very open-minded, but I don’t know how this is going to go.”</p><h3><b>Ramirez sits again</b></h3><p>The Cubs kept infielder <b>Pedro Ramirez</b> out of the lineup for a third consecutive game Wednesday as he recovers from back spasms that popped up Sunday.</p><p>“I expect him to make a full recovery and be good entries.title: Playing time could be sparse for White Sox' right-handed outfielders down the stretch
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON — <b>Randal Grichuk</b>’s two-run double off Astros reliever <b>Tatsuya Imai</b> broke open the White Sox’ 5-1 victory on Tuesday. But the bigger development was Grichuk getting an opportunity to face right-handed pitching at all.</p><p>The 35-year-old’s brilliance as a midseason pickup has been his ability to mash left-handed pitching on command. While his spot in the lineup against right-handed starter <b>Ronel Blanco</b> was partially about a rest day for rookie <b>Braden Montgomery</b>, it also was about not letting Grichuk rust during a long absence of traditional opportunities.</p><p>“Minnesota, back home, it’s going to be all righties,” Grichuk said of the coming series against the Twins. “Sprinkle some at-bats in, to where it’s not a huge layoff, definitely huge for feel and the rhythm.”</p><p>Manager <b>Will Venable</b> loves playing platoon matchups, and hunting value on the margins remains vital as the Sox push to clinch the American League Central title. Simultaneously, the presence of newly acquired right-handed outfielders <b>Brenton Doyle</b> and <b>Tommy Pham</b>,<b> </b>alongside Grichuk, give the Sox a host of players they want to keep active in some form.</p><p>“We’re going to have to figure out how to keep them involved,” Venable said. “There will be [pinch-hit] opportunities during the game. I’m not sure exactly how we’ll get them starts, to be honest.”</p><p>To drive the point home, Venable admitted utilityman Luisangel Acuña likely won’t start a game all this week.</p><p>“We’ve been transparent with them about what it looks like for them over this next stretch,” Venable said.</p><h3><b>From opening day starter to Triple-A reliever</b></h3><p><b>Shane Smith</b>’s last two outings with Triple-A Charlotte have been in relief, as the White Sox abandon ideas of restoring his place in the rotation this year. Those outings have also both been scoreless.</p><p>“He's an option,” Venable said of Smith’s chances of contributing to the major league bullpen. “I was looking at videos today, I think he looks really good.”</p><h3><b>Vasil has a date</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Dugout cheerleader extraordinaire <b>Mike Vasil </b>rushed from the airport to the ballpark Tuesday night to celebrate a victory with teammates, but he also had personal reasons to smile. Vasil’s visit to Dr. Keith Meister in Dallas saw him cleared to play catch on Sept. 18, which will be his first time throwing since undergoing Tommy John surgery.</p><p>“As much fun as I’ve had, it’s not even close to the same as actually playing,” Vasil said.</p><h3><b>Brazoban begins rehab</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Eight days after being placed on the injured list with a strained left lat muscle, right-handed reliever <b>Huascar Brazoban</b> began a Triple-A rehab assignment on Wednesday.</p><p>That normally would suggest a swift return for an important White Sox trade-deadline acquisition, but Brazoban allowed six runs in his last five innings before his injury, and the Sox want to see a return to form before he’s activated.</p><p>“The key with him is execute the changeup,” pitching coach Zach Bove told the Sun-Times. “So [hitters] have to honor something else. Because if not, then he’s boxed into being pretty much a one-pitch guy.”</p><h3><b>Bush and Berroa update</b></h3><h3></h3><p>After both underwent Tommy John surgery in spring 2025, <b>Ky Bush </b>and <b>Prelander Berroa</b> have also been sidelined all this year with setbacks in their rehab process.</p><p>Bush is officially done for the season due to a left lat strain, while Berroa will throw off a mound again next week for the first time since May.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Gloria Steinem, a potent voice of US feminism and co-founder of Ms. Magazine, dies at 92
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK (AP) — Gloria Steinem, the celebrated author and activist who became one of the most visible symbols and potent voices of the U.S. women’s movement and a fierce advocate for feminist causes throughout her life, has died. She was 92.</p><p>With her trademark streaked hair parted down the middle and large aviator glasses, Steinem, a co-founder of Ms. Magazine, was a hugely recognizable presence wherever she went. And she went everywhere: Much of her life as an advocate was spent on the road, speaking at college campuses and community centers, at rallies and marches.</p><p>She died Wednesday at her home in New York City, according to her and her foundation’s social media pages.</p><p>“Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard,” the posts said. “Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor.”</p><p>Steinem enjoyed writing and spending time in the community in recent years, the posts said. She also hosted talking circles for hundreds of people in her home. She died just before a planned memoir was to be released this fall.</p><p>“You can’t do it on the phone or on the web,” she told The Associated Press <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/dd3f1c7be0c4463da2a5aa58e59be342" target="_blank" >in a 2015 interview.</a> “You have to be there with all five senses. It should be obvious that people can’t empathize with each other unless we’re in the same room.”</p><h4>Steinem changed her career path after a start as a journalist</h4><p>She began her career as a journalist, notably one who reported, in 1963, on degrading conditions in Hugh Hefner’s Playboy empire, an undercover assignment she came to later regret. She credits a meeting six years later, where women spoke out boldly in favor of abortion rights, with changing her career path.</p><p>“That speak-out was the beginning of activism for me,” Steinem, who had undergone a secret illegal abortion herself at age 22, told the AP in an email in 2022, <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/abortion-us-supreme-court-health-gloria-steinem-government-and-politics-5b174a67f33902328198c8493290dd42" target="_blank" >reflecting on the reversal of Roe v Wade.</a> “Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we’re not living in a democracy.”</p><p>Though she soon became a known activist, those who watched Steinem denounce discrimination for so many years likely never suspected that she’d had to overcome a deep fear of public speaking. She would have simply stuck to writing, she said, if only editors at the time had been willing to let her write about the women’s movement.</p><p>But they weren’t interested, she told the AP in 2015. “So I ended up going out and speaking, which was my nightmare,” she said. “I mean, I was terrified. But I’m grateful, even though I still get scared even now.”</p><h4>Steinem’s visibility endured throughout her life</h4><p>Time hardly slowed Steinem down; well into her 80s she was traveling the globe and speaking out on issues of importance to her. These included everything from genital mutilation to Korean reconciliation, but it was equality for women that took precedence. “Being a feminist means that you see the world as whole instead of half,” she once said. “It shouldn’t need a name, and one day it won’t.”</p><p>As the years went on, Steinem’s visibility endured. At 83, she sat in the front row of her first fashion show, guest of designer Prabal Gurung. A few days after her 85th birthday, she was leading a women’s “talking circle” at an off-Broadway play celebrating her life, where one by one, women in the audience — many fighting tears — rose to thank her and tell their own stories of discrimination. In 2020, her life was the subject of a feature film, “The Glorias, A Life on The Road,” based on her 2015 memoir and starring Julianne Moore.</p><p>And at 91, <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/gloria-steinem-leymah-gbowee-picture-book-6b66128d908604856e227a5ff9784ab0" target="_blank" >she collaborated on a picture book</a> with Liberian peace activist and Nobel laureate Leymah Gbowee aimed at inspiring young people to change the world. “Rise, Girl, Rise: Our Sister-Friend Journey. Together for All” was published in February 2026.</p><p>The constant visibility came with a price; even into her older years, Steinem expressed frustration that despite her accomplishments, she was often described as beautiful or glamorous (A 1992 Vanity Fair profile even noted her “spectacular racehorse legs.”) It was a label she said unfairly detracted from her message.</p><p>“Nobody ever called me beautiful until I was publicly a feminist, and that was in my mid-30s,” she told AP in a 2011 interview. “It was clear that label was being assigned to me. The most hurtful part is that you work very hard, and people say it’s because of your looks.”</p><h4>Steinem dealt with hostility from many directions</h4><p>Of course, Steinem also had to deal with hostility. Sometimes it came from surprising places. Appearing on Larry King’s talk show on CNN in 1990, she was visibly stunned when a female caller greeted her cheerfully, then told her to “rot in hell” because she had ruined “the beautiful American family.”</p><p>But by then, she noted, at least people were taking feminists seriously. That wasn’t the case in 1972 when she co-founded Ms. Magazine and many commentators — especially male — dismissed it as ridiculous, predicting an early demise. (The magazine continues to this day, published by the Feminist Majority Foundation.)</p><p>Among Steinem’s detractors was President Richard Nixon, who was caught on an Oval Office tape ridiculing both her and the “Ms.” title. The ridicule was mutual: In a 1972 National Press Club speech, Steinem called Nixon “the most sexually insecure chief of state since Napoleon.”</p><p>It was just one example of Steinem’s trademark wit. Before she married at 66, she often explained her singlehood by saying “I can’t mate in captivity.” Laughter, she wrote, was “the only free emotion — the only one that can’t be compelled.”</p>

entries.title: Trump's ballroom is a monument to his lawlessness
entries.summary: <p>After President Theodore Roosevelt began building the East Wing of the White House in 1902, he <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/GPO-CRECB-1903-pt1-v36-2-1.pdf#page=6" target="_blank" >thanked</a> Congress for approving the project and appropriating the necessary funds. When President Donald Trump demolished the East Wing last fall, by contrast, he acted without permission from Congress, which the Constitution empowers to control federal property.</p><p>That difference is unlikely to matter in practice, thanks to a stay the Supreme Court <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-white-house-ballroom-supreme-court-6b9434af0a2dbeffa0ca19f5cdf7d775" target="_blank" >issued</a> Monday, which allows Trump to continue work on the huge ballroom he is building on the site of the East Wing. But Trump's insistence on acting unilaterally will make his vanity project a monument to his disregard for the rule of law and the separation of powers.</p><p>In an <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/26a203_2b8e.pdf" target="_blank" >unsigned opinion</a> joined by five justices, the Supreme Court blocked a preliminary injunction against continued construction of the ballroom, which the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/10/d-c-circuit-upholds-injunction-against-trumps-ballroom/" target="_blank" >upheld</a> in August after concluding that Congress had not authorized the project. But the justices said they were not addressing the legality of the ballroom.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c70000" name="module-c70000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Rather, the court issued the stay because the majority thought the government was likely to prevail in its claim that the main plaintiff, the National Trust for Historic Preservation, lacked standing to sue. In a <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/26a203_2b8e.pdf#page=9" target="_blank" >dissent</a> joined by the court's three Democratic appointees, Chief Justice John Roberts disagreed, saying the "aesthetic injury" asserted by architectural historian Alison Hoagland, a member of the National Trust, was enough to pass that test.</p><p>Unlike the majority, Roberts did venture an opinion about whether the ballroom project is legal. By issuing the stay, he complained, the court was "allowing the Executive's likely infringement of the Legislature's power of the purse and authority to regulate federal property in the District of Columbia to continue."</p><p>That characterization was consistent with what U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, a George W. Bush appointee, <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/04/06/with-his-grandiose-white-house-ballroom-plan-trump-again-asserts-the-power-to-do-as-he-pleases/" target="_blank" >said</a> when he issued the injunction at issue in this case last March. "The President of the United States is the steward of the White House for future generations of First Families," Leon <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/04/06/with-his-grandiose-white-house-ballroom-plan-trump-again-asserts-the-power-to-do-as-he-pleases/" target="_blank" >wrote</a>. "He is not, however, the owner!"</p><p>The National Trust "is likely to succeed on the merits because no statute comes close to giving the President the authority he claims," Leon concluded. The D.C. Circuit <a class="Link" href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/73127510/national-trust-for-historic-preservation-v-nps/" target="_blank" >agreed</a>, saying "whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide" rather than "a matter for Executive self-help."</p><p>Under <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/40/8106" target="_blank" >federal law</a>, "a building or structure shall not be erected on any reservation, park, or public grounds of the Federal Government in the District of Columbia without express authority of Congress."</p><p>In lieu of such express authority, Trump cited two laws: one <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/3/105" target="_blank" >allowing</a> the president to spend appropriated money on maintenance of "the Executive Residence at the White House," the other <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/54/100101" target="_blank" >instructing</a> the National Park Service to "conserve … historic objects" under its control, including the White House.</p><p>By combining those two laws, Trump asserted, he could do whatever he wanted with the White House, such as using $400 million in privately donated funds to replace the East Wing with a new structure that will be 60% larger than the executive residence in square footage and more than three times as large in cubic volume. Like Leon and the D.C. Circuit, Roberts was skeptical.</p><p>The first law, under which Congress allocated $2.5 million for White House maintenance this fiscal year, "likely does not authorize the President to use hundreds of millions of dollars in private donations to tear down the East Wing and construct a ballroom in its stead," Roberts said. The second law, he added, "is likely not express authorization to raze the East Wing and replace it with a ballroom."</p><p>The project, in other words, is probably illegal. But it should be clear by now that Trump, who has illegally <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/02/20/the-supreme-court-just-struck-down-trumps-emergency-tariffs/" target="_blank" >imposed</a> tariffs, <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/06/22/the-attack-on-iran-is-unlawful/" target="_blank" >waged war</a> against Iran, <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/12/24/refusing-to-let-trump-deploy-the-national-guard-in-chicago-scotus-adds-a-new-wrinkle-to-the-debate/" target="_blank" >deployed</a> the National Guard and <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/22/trumps-threats-to-yank-broadcast-licenses-are-part-of-a-speech-chilling-intimidation-campaign/" target="_blank" >used</a> his powers to <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/05/28/a-federal-judge-lists-8-ways-that-trump-violated-the-constitution-by-punishing-a-disfavored-law-firm/" target="_blank" >retaliate</a> against his <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/30/trump-loves-accusing-critics-of-treason-u-s-law-makes-that-charge-hard-to-prove-for-good-reason/" target="_blank" >political opponents</a>, is unfazed by such considerations.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-420000" name="module-420000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: Jacob Sullum

entries.title: Dear Abby: Widow's new beau does not pull his weight
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband died six years ago. I met a widower three years ago. He was nice and attentive, but not anymore. We moved in together, and the last two years I have been miserable.</p><p>I pay half the rent. I also pay for all the groceries and gas and pick up the check every time we go out to eat. He even takes my meds, so I have only half of what I need. The only time he is not moody is when I wait on him hand and foot.</p><p>I have nothing. I live on Social Security, and so does he. He doesn't hit or abuse me, so I feel like I should stay, yet I'm so unhappy. He doesn't talk to me or even give me a hug. I think I'm stuck and don't know where to turn. My grown kids don't need to hear that I messed up, and I don't want to burden them. Can you please advise me? — <i>MISERABLE IN ARIZONA</i></p><p><b>DEAR MISERABLE:</b> Gladly. Your grown children need to know exactly what your situation is with this man. Whose name is on the lease of your dwelling? If it isn't you, there is no reason why you can't end this pain. Tell your kids what's going on and ask for their help in getting out of this soul-crushing mess. It may be embarrassing, but it may be the only way to escape.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I will be attending my nephew's wedding in the northeast part of the country. I live in the mid-Atlantic. I have been told that at the reception each plate will cost $200, and they are expecting their wedding gifts to be worth at least the cost of the plate. Therefore, if a couple attends and both spouses dine at the reception, a $400 wedding gift is expected. Are these guidelines for real? — <i>BAFFLED ABOUT ALL THIS</i></p><p><b>DEAR BAFFLED:</b> These "guidelines" do not exist except in the minds of the presumptuous individuals who are throwing this shindig. A wedding reception is not a quid pro quo affair. The cost of the celebration is borne by the bride and groom and their parents, and no one else. If you plan to attend, your wedding gift should not cost more than you can comfortably afford.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I lost my wife in November to non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) that had progressed to cirrhosis. She also had polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), which was diagnosed in 1990. No doctor told my wife in the intervening years, "You have PCOS, so you need to get your liver checked." For some reason, most general practitioners and OB-GYNs do not tell their patients this.</p><p>According to the World Health Organization, about 10% of women have PCOS. According to the National Institutes of Health, between 34% and 70% of PCOS patients develop fatty liver disease. Could you use your platform to tell PCOS patients to advocate for themselves to get liver scans done? I don't want any other family to experience the loss that my family has. — <i>WARNING TO WOMEN</i></p><p><b>DEAR WARNING TO WOMEN:</b> Please accept my sympathy for the loss of your wife to this terrible disease. Readers, I can't promise insurance will pay for the additional testing for all PCOS patients, but it can't hurt to raise the subject with your doctor.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Sound & Gravity festival: Breaking down year two with creator Mike Reed
entries.summary: <p>There's only one way to sum up the eclectic range of acts appearing at the Sound & Gravity Festival this weekend, a lineup that includes electro rockers Son Lux, ambient master Grouper and avant-jazz ensemble Natural Information Society.</p><p>“The band has either played at Constellation or should have,” said festival creator Mike Reed.</p><p>The boutique venue, 3111 N. Western Ave., is where Reed books a mix of modern jazz, contemporary classical and experimental acts year-round. And it’s one of the seven concert halls participating in the multiday, multivenue festival that returns Sept. 3-6 to the Avondale area for its second year. Other participating spots within a 2-mile radius include Reed’s other venue Hungry Brain, 2319 W. Belmont Ave., as well as Beat Kitchen, 2100 W. Belmont Ave.; Judson & Moore, 3057 N. Rockwell St.; Guild Row, 3130 N. Rockwell; and Rockwell on the River and its adjoining patio, 3057 N. Rockwell St.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7d0000" name="module-7d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Sound & Gravity </h3><b>When:</b> Sept. 3-6<br><b>Where:</b> Multiple venues<br><b>Tickets:</b> $56.99+ for single day pass; $253.88 for 4-day pass (venue-only tickets are also available)<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://soundandgravity.org/" target="_blank" >soundandgravity.org</a></div> </div><p>New this year is adding the Athenaeum Theatre, 2936 N. Southport Ave. in Lake View. “It gives us a larger, 950-capacity theater and the chance to experiment in working with them and maybe have more Constellation or Sound & Gravity shows another time of the year,” Reed said. </p><p>Programming the festival in one centralized area of venues (where Reed also lives) is twofold. First, he said, “I wanted to get away from the festival of 20,000 people in the park, which I think has in a lot of ways played itself out, at least in Chicago.”</p><p>But the other reason was to encourage music fans to easily jump from one venue to the next and discover a new band — or a new neighborhood. Sound & Gravity’s website offers a map with eight different restaurants to check out nearby, too, like Indian street food eatery Thattu and BBQ hot spot Soul & Smoke.</p><p>“The core of our audience is people who are interested in discovery,” said Reed. It’s the same community he once attracted with the now-shuttered Pitchfork Music Fest, which he co-produced since its inception in 2006, or the acts he booked for the Downtown Sound Music Series in Millennium Park every summer.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b20000" audience.”</p><p>As Reed has found, audiences are hungry for that experience. The inaugural festival in 2025 drew in music fans from 36 states and six countries, including Canada and the UK, and more artists have been requesting spots on future lineups. “I have submissions for next year's festival, and we haven't even done round two yet,” said Reed, who's also a career musician. His latest album with the Separatist Party comes out Oct. 23 on local label Thrill Jockey.</p><p>As such, supporting the local scene has become just as important when booking Sound & Gravity. “One of the things I wanted to do a little bit more this year was to try and get some younger [local] acts,” he said, referencing lo-fi indie rockers Leroy the Poet (featuring Pavement front man Stephen Malkmus' daughter Lottie), DIY troupe TV Buddha and post-punk trio Uniflora. “I hope by doing so, some of the younger artists will maybe start seeing themselves in the music that's happening here."</p><p>Sound & Gravity Festival serves another important role in the local music economy: It’s a fundraising machine for the nonprofit side of Constellation Performing Arts, which Reed set up in 2013 in tandem with buying the former Viaduct Theatre space that’s now home to Constellation. “We just figured instead of us doing a black-tie gala or some fundraising campaign, how about we just make an event [like Sound & Gravity] that asks for a bit of a premium, but also gives a lot to choose from with these artists coming together,” said Reed, who recommends “taste testing” all the lineup has to offer with the full festival pass. Single-day and single venue passes are also available.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Jenkins</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>That funding allows him to keep offering a platform to host the city’s avant-garde music community that might otherwise fight for space. One of the benefactors is the local instrumental rock trio Black Duck, who performs Sunday at Judson & Moore.</p><p>“Events like these remind people of the vibrancy of what we have in Chicago. It’s such a different thing than what I think of as a mainstream festival, in this country anyway … and I'm glad Mike got it up and running,” said Black Duck guitarist Bill MacKay, who is joined in the group by bassist/guitarist Douglas McCombs (also of Tortoise) and drummer Charles Rumback.</p><p>MacKay likens Reed to a “great connector” who once hired him and Rumback for respective instrument tech and production manager roles at Pitchfork Music Fest and introduced the band to producer Nick Broste, who worked on their latest collaborative album, “Black Duck with Elena Setién,” released Aug. 28. “Mike’s just such a great lover of music … and it’s crazy how deep the connections go,” added Rumback.</p><p>“Spaces like [Sound & Gravity] that really make room for left of center art are important,” said Alex E. Chávez, singer/guitarist of Chicago-based Dos Santos. The alt-Latinx band that experiments with the roots of cumbia will perform Thursday at Rockwell Patio. “It really elevates the kind of homespun, organic, grassroots music cultures that exist in our communities and shows we are open to so many things.”</p><p>Chávez, a professor of anthropology by day at the University of Notre Dame, has often researched this intersection of music and community, which has become a recurring theme on the quintet’s music, including its fourth album, “Es Amor,” released Aug. 28. </p><p>“Having an event like this does the really important work of continuing to put Chicago on the map as one of the most important music cities in the U.S.,” he said. “It just takes people [like Mike] doing the work and opening up the spaces for that to happen.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d20000" name="module-d20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>5 more acts to add to your Sound & Gravity schedule</h3><br><b>If you like Sonic Youth, check out Lee Ranaldo & Leah Singer, Contre Jour (Saturday at Constellation)</b><br><br>Ranaldo was the longtime guitarist of the New York noise rockers, but in his current project with multimedia artist Leah Singer, they create large-scale sonic murals using a combination of light, film and sound.<br><br><b>If you like The Dirty Three, check out Mick Turner (Thursday, Constellation) and Jim White Trio (Friday, Beat Kitchen)</b><br><br>Both Turner and White were part of the Australian post-rock band and bring the same kind of musicality and contemplative opuses into their solo projects. In White’s trio, he’s joined by Fugazi’s Guy Picciotto and Colleen Burke of ’90s Chicago band We Ragazzi.<br><br><b>If you like Black Midi, check out My New Band Believe (Saturday, Beat Kitchen)</b><br><br>This art-rock group is quite literally the new band of Black Midi bassist and singer Cameron Picton after his former group went on hiatus in 2024. His latest project plays with the same progressive style and a bit more acoustic and whimsical compositions.<br><br><b>If you like Animal Collective or Devendra Banhart, check out Sir Richard Bishop (Sunday, Judson & Moore)</b><br><br>The accomplished guitarist and composer has a long history of touring with those acts as well as Bill Callahan and Bonnie “Prince” Billy.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Evanston’s new Northlight Theatre is built for new plays
entries.summary: <p>As theaters around the country, including Broadway, continue to struggle, one Chicago suburb is cutting the ribbon on yet another multimillion dollar venue in the area.</p><p>You can’t miss Evanston’s new $32 million Northlight Theatre. Situated near both CTA and Metra train stations, with its two-story glass walls facing outward, the building is the result of concerted efforts to integrate the theater company into the neighborhood and create an arts anchor.</p><p>“We wanted to design a building that fit into Evanston, but also was distinctive,” said Northlight Executive Director Tim Evans. “It has an industrial sort of feel to it and look to it because we make art in here, but we also wanted it to have a bit of a contemporary flair.”</p><p>It took more than a decade to get here. The initial idea started with a study by the National Endowment for the Arts to design an arts district in downtown Evanston that included Northlight’s return. Founded in Evanston in the 1970s, Northlight has spent recent years in nearby Skokie.</p><p>Evans, whose theater company has an annual budget around $5.25 million, said the project wouldn't have made it across the finish line without support from the community.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" has embraced us,” he said. “We have about 625 major donors who donated to the building itself, and 72% of those are from Evanston, so it has become a place of pride for Evanston.” (The State of Illinois and the city of Evanston also contributed.)</p><p>The 24,000-square-foot building features plenty of bells-and-whistles, including 150,000 pounds of structural and catwalk steel. But the key component of the space is the theater itself.</p><p>“The most important thing is that the audience feels like they’re in the journey of the play. That’s the gift and that’s part of what having a bespoke theater is all about,” said Northlight Artistic Director BJ Jones.</p><p>It’s a Tuesday morning, weeks before opening night of the inaugural show, “The Front Page,” which Jones will direct. At the moment, the new auditorium sits empty.</p><p>A “bespoke theater,” which Jones refers to, simply means a custom-designed performance space that was built from scratch. The 287 seats that surround Jones as he speaks these words are state of the art. They’re noticeably larger than typical theater seats and have extra legroom, yet the auditorium maintains a feeling of intimacy. incorporating the theater into the urban setting of downtown Evanston.</p><p>“You have a lot of glass on the facade, so that as you walk by, or as you approach the building, it's all very transparent,” said Smith. “You can see in, and when you’re inside, you can see out and see the community and neighborhood. That was very important.”</p><p>But one challenge to contend with was noise, from the neighboring Metra and CTA stations to nearby Northwestern University and daily Downtown foot and car traffic. “We had to acoustically seal and make sure we're isolated enough that that didn't affect the action on stage,” Smith said. “Also, leaning toward intimacy, the acoustics allow for actors to talk without supplemental electronic enhancement as much as possible.”</p><p>Even with all the new upgrades — which include large greenrooms for actors, rehearsal space, a loading dock and a costume shop — the theater still has about the same amount of seats as its former location. When building a theater from scratch, why not put 1,000 seats?</p><p>Jones said the answer is simple: “We make new work,” he explained. “And to have a big theater puts a greater financial risk on it. We'd rather create the work in its infancy and let it grow, and then, if it has the kind of success that every artist hopes for, then it can move on to bigger spaces and other cities. But, we're really an incubator for new and fresh work.”</p><p>For Evans, the communal aspect was important. “We want to be a community center, a third space, and a public square for all sorts of ideas,” he said. He mentioned the proximity to Northwestern University and the possibility of hosting lectures and TED Talks. He also said he’d like to invite fellow theater companies to use the stage and could potentially host film festivals.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" When Northlight purchased its building, they also acquired an adjoining restaurant, owned by a big name in the Chicago food scene.</p><p>“The Barn is now a tenant of ours,” said Evans. “Amy Morton is the proprietor and has been for a while. So there's a steakhouse connected to the theater.”</p><p>In the future, both Evans and Jones see Northlight as a hub for arts in Evanston.</p><p>“Since we've started building, the city of Evanston has decided that this is going to be an arts district,” said Evans. “I think that’s economic stimulation. Arts and culture wants to be an economic driver in the community and is seen as something that can raise all boats in Evanston.”</p><p>Evans said that there are about 7,000 people who live within four blocks of the theater that create a "built-in audience.” Already, Northlight has doubled its season subscribers from last year, he added, but his ultimate takeaway for the new venue is what it says about Chicago theater as an industry.</p><p>“There are more theaters being built in Chicago than anywhere else right now,” he said, including the new <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/04/03/in-uptown-timeline-theatre-moves-into-its-new-home-nearly-a-decade-in-the-making" target="_blank" ><u>TimeLine Theater</u></a>, which opened last year, and Edgewater’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2025/12/12/steep-theatre-new-home-edgewater-black-box-theater" target="_blank" ><u>Steep Theatre</u></a>, which broke ground on its new building in December. “I think that reflects the attitude of the audiences in this town. It's a great theater town. It's a great actor town. It's a great director town. So we're booming.”</p>

entries.title: 3 leaders who work with Chicago's immigrant communities reflect on the toll of Operation Midway Blitz
entries.summary: <p>Not leaving your home for days or weeks. Always being on the lookout to protect yourself and your loved ones. It can lead to a constant state of fear, stress, even hopelessness.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2026/07/24/chaotic-crowded-chicago-immigration-mega-court-hearings-are-fueling-record-deportation-orders" target="_blank" ><u>Over the last year</u></a>, immigrants in many communities in Chicago and the suburbs have experienced such a rollercoaster of emotions as federal immigration agents have detained people without legal immigration status and others who also were swept up in arrests as part of President Donald Trump’s mass-deportation campaign.</p><p>They're not the only ones to have been left reeling. People trying to help them have felt this, too — community leaders, social workers and people who provide mental health services for immigrants and their families.</p><p>“Secondary trauma was so pervasive," says Mauricio Cifuentes, director of programs for the Family Service and Mental Health Center of Cicero.</p><p>Many of these helpers are immigrants themselves, with stories of their own families’ journeys to the United States. These are the stories of three of them. They speak of how Operation Midway Blitz has affected them and what they do to cope.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cindy Eigler, the executive director of the Coalition for Immigrant Mental Health, says she works out her stress by boxing.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Boxing as a lifeline</h3><p>At the height of <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2025/09/10/operation-midway-blitz-deportation-campaign-chicago-donald-trump-gregory-bovino" target="_blank" ><u>Midway Blitz</u></a> in the fall of 2025, Cindy Eigler would open her phone and see hundreds of messages on rapid response threads reporting ICE sightings and activity around the north suburbs.</p><p>“It was taking up all of my brain space,” says Eigler, who lives in Evanston. “I wasn't sleeping, and I was really grumpy with my kids and snapping at them at things that I shouldn't be and then just feeling really helpless.”</p><p>She’s kept a whistle by her front door and in her car since she regularly responded to sightings of federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, often at Home Depot stores and other locations migrants might gather. It was part of her volunteer work with a rapid response team trying to stay on top of sightings of immigration agents. She also assisted with the aftermath of immigration enforcement, helping families whose relatives were detained to get aid to pay for rent and food.</p><p>“That was really heavy but super-important,” Eigler says.</p><p>She felt overwhelmed. </p><p>Her entire world — 24 hours a day — was taken over by Operation Midway Blitz. It was her volunteer work and her day job.</p><p>Eigler is executive director of the not-for-profit <a class="Link" href="https://www.ourcimh.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Coalition for Immigrant Mental Health</u></a>. A key part of her job is preventing mental health crises by<b> </b>creating mostly virtual healing spaces for immigrants, refugees and frontline staff workers of organizations that work with them to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/06/17/immigrant-refugee-communities-invisible-backpack-worry-fear-enforcement-mental-health-aimee-hilado" target="_blank" ><u>help process what they’ve seen and experienced.</u></a> She says she's trying to help people understand what trauma is, how it affects their health and how to manage it.</p><p>Eigler used to work with survivors of police torture. So she says she’s heard horrible stories before. But Midway Blitz felt different. It hit close to home.</p><p>Eigler’s parents came to the United States from Venezuela while her mother was pregnant with her. Her father’s family were refugees who escaped the Holocaust, and her mother’s family traces their roots to Egypt and Palestine.</p><p>Growing up, Eigler’s family didn’t talk about pain, rage or sadness.</p><p>“The trauma that they've experienced and not always having that feeling of belonging or being ostracized or discriminated against, that shows up in how they are and how they move in the world,” she says.</p><p>She says her mother has lived in the United States for nearly 50 years and yet "she still gets told all the time to go back to where she comes from."</p><p>Eigler says she used to try to hold in her feelings. But, for the past decade, she has found an outlet to try to release them: boxing. </p><p>“What I was taught from a young age was: You just put your head down and you just take it, and you just try to help other people and not say what you need," she says. "Boxing was the first time where I was, like, ‘Oh, I get to really have a desire or a need or a power. ’”</p><p>Eigler knew the constant updates in her rapid response thread set off hypervigilant feelings for her. It took about three months to realize it was too much. She stepped back from the rapid response movement and says, as a result, she soon felt more present as a parent and at the coalition.</p><p>Eigler has now started a program to <a class="Link" href="https://www.ourcimh.org/community-resources" target="_blank" ><u>embed mental health support</u></a> inside community organizations to offer that help at places where people already feel safe, among those they trust.</p><p>The coalition develops programming with partner organizations and designs it to respond to a community's particular needs, from training on secondary traumatic stress to art or yoga. There are <a class="Link" href="https://www.ourcimh.org/cimh-resources" target="_blank" ><u>healing circles</u></a> and listening spaces with the goal of providing a place where people can feel free to process what they are carrying and feel heard in community.</p><p>A year since Midway Blitz began, Eigler says she is still consumed by and passionate about her work. Immigrants still fear what could happen to them and their families. She says she thinks a lot about how to make sure their mental health is a priority. She says trauma can unfold for generations.</p><p>“You have good days, and you have days that feel harder and when you feel more pessimistic and more cynical about what is happening,” Eigler says. “It helps me a lot to be at an organization where I can be in motion with other people and be trying to support in the ways that we can and be in action.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Angela Sedeño, the executive director of the LoSAH Center of Hope, a bilingual mental health clinic serving Logan Square, Avondale and Hermosa with affordable mental health services in English and Spanish.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez / WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Hoping to ‘regain our bearings’</h3><p>Angela Sedeño was on her way to the bank last October when she learned <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/10/03/federal-agent-chemical-irritants-rico-fresh-logan-square" target="_blank" ><u>tear gas had been deployed </u></a>outside Rico Fresh Market in Logan Square in front of the LoSAH Center of Hope, the bilingual mental health clinic where she is executive director.</p><p>She saw people running for shelter. She rushed to check on her neighbors. She still can’t shake the memory of seeing two of her youngest staff members come inside with watering, bloodshot eyes from the gas and how she felt she couldn't protect them.</p><p>“It was just things that we didn’t prepare for, that we couldn’t have seen coming,” Sedeño says. “We have all of these emergency and crisis plans for all sorts of other things, like mental health crises, but certainly not those types of tactics being used in the street.”</p><p>The LoSAH center is a community-funded clinic that serves Logan Square, Avondale and Hermosa with affordable mental health services in English and Spanish, including therapy, support groups and collective healing practices like sound baths and drum circles.</p><p>Sedeño’s role encompasses everything from forming community partnerships and overseeing clinical services to providing community interventions and trying to stay on top of the community’s mental health needs.</p><p>The responsibility of serving the center’s clients and also her staff can be a lot even in ordinary times. But the uncertainty and violence of Midway Blitz took a steep toll on her employees, half of them bicultural and bilingual themselves, as they sat in with clients experiencing panic, fear and despair while navigating their own feelings of rage and helplessness.</p><p>Sedeño says she tries to make sure that her staff members take breaks and aren’t overburdened. She says she uses a practice called reflective supervision to create spaces for people to share and process their feelings with the help of trained supervisors.</p><p>“Everything we would do for a client, we’re also doing for our staff,” says Sedeño, a first-generation Mexican American.</p><p>“Growing up brown in the United States meant that, at different points of my life as a child, there was discrimination for skin color, for language,” Sedeño says. “And so, seeing all of this happening so blatantly, it’s heartbreaking. It’s heartbreaking to hear the stories and to see the faces that look like you being targeted.”</p><p>To care for herself, she leans on a therapist, her family, her faith and the LoSAH center’s many community partners.</p><p>With the new school year starting and the uncertainty that can bring, Sedeño and her staff are bracing to support families as their fears, anxieties and traumas resurface.</p><p>“I would hope that at some point we regain our bearings and people have an opportunity to rest and recover because that hasn’t happened yet,” Sedeño says.</p><div class="Enhancement"
