class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez ? Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Bringing calm, hope back </h3><p>Little Village, the predominantly Mexican American Southwest Side neighborhood, was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2026/02/20/operation-midway-blitz-effects-latino-neighborhoods-pilsen-little-village-southeast-side" target="_blank" ><u>at the center </u></a>of immigration enforcement operations last fall. Whirring helicopters and whistles warning that immigration agents were near became the norm.</p><p>Vero Ortiz, senior director of community wellness for the not-for-profit organization Enlace Chicago in Little Village, remembers it this way: “There were days that you wouldn’t see anybody on the streets. There was just so much fear. And now we’re living in the underbelly of that fear.”</p><p>While fewer agents roam the streets and enforcement has become more targeted, Ortiz says the psychological impact persists.</p><p>Ortiz lives in the suburbs and has worked for Enlace for two years but identifies as someone “adopted by Little Village.” As a first-generation Mexican American, Ortiz speaks to having a strong cultural connection to the neighborhood, which is why having to fight a system Ortiz says is trying to erase the vibrant community has prompted grief, anger and stress.</p><p>“I cried this morning,” Ortiz says. “I saw a post of a little girl standing between an ICE agent and her mom, right? It’s still happening.”</p><p>Ortiz’s powerful emotions, however, have not hindered their work. Rather, they fuel it, with a drive to offer more preventative options to help residents be empowered and ready for the next crisis.</p><p>Ortiz has been working to meet the surge in need for mental health services. They secured city funding this year for an additional community-based therapist and a school-based therapist as well as for a new family support specialist who could help, for instance, people who might still be afraid to leave their homes. <i> </i></p><p>“We can sometimes work at 100 miles an hour even though, as leaders, we’re not asking our staff to do it,” says Ortiz, who has worked in child welfare and gang intervention. “I think they do it because they love what they do. So it’s also my responsibility to be, like, ‘Hey, I’m going to need you to not burn yourself out’ because I need my staff to be well in order for us to serve the community.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Feixu Chen</i></p><p><i>Mary Ellen Ritter and Navya Shukla produced this story as part of the Medill Investigative Lab-Chicago at Northwestern University.</i></p><p><i>This story was produced as part of the</i><a class="Link" href="https://mentalhealthjournalism.org/parity-collaborative/" target="_blank" ><i> <u>Mental Health Parity Collaborative</u></i></a><i>, a group of newsrooms and universities covering mental health care access and inequities in the United States.</i><br></p>

entries.title: How does Chicago’s cultural spending compare to other cities?
entries.summary: <p>New York City’s buzzy progressive mayor, Zohran Mamdani, took to social media last month to announce — <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/16/nyregion/mamdani-mandarin-video.html?unlocked_article_code=1.6FA.y-v3.m0wB9a7x4XGy&smid=nytcore-ios-share" target="_blank" ><u>in multiple languages</u></a> — an initiative to give thousands of free Broadway tickets to local high school students.</p><p>Paired with a recent, <a class="Link" href="https://www.artforum.com/news/mamdani-allocates-a-record-323-million-for-culture-1234753986/" target="_blank" ><u>record-setting $323.8 million</u></a> allocated for New York’s Department of Cultural Affairs in the city’s budget, Mamdani appears intent on building a reputation as a culture-forward mayor. His enthusiasm comes as <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/05/03/nx-s1-5385888/sweeping-cuts-hit-nea-after-trump-administration-calls-to-eliminate-the-agency" target="_blank" ><u>federal arts support</u></a> has withered under President Donald Trump, and as private foundations that buttress the arts shift their priorities elsewhere. That’s made local government investment more critical than ever.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> <div id="Form-newsletter-wrapper" class="Form-newsletter-wrapper" strong support. Now, three years into Mayor Brandon Johnson’s term, as the city heads into its fall budget season and gears up for a mayoral election, WBEZ/Sun-Times asked advocates and the mayor himself about the city’s commitment to the arts and crunched the numbers to look at how Chicago’s budget stacks up compared to other major cities.</p><p>Across the country’s five largest cities (New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston and Phoenix), Chicago was the only one to cut the funding for its local arts agency during its most recent budget cycle. And while its spending dwarfs that of the larger Los Angeles, and trails only behind New York in per capita arts dollars, the pressure is mounting on city leaders to do more.</p><p>“I don't like to compare myself to any other place because there's just no comparison to the cultural, the art scene in Chicago,” Johnson said in an interview last week about arts under his leadership. “What I can say, though, is for me, making the investments in arts and culture, that I believe is the way to define my administration.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-8b0000" name="html-embed-module-8b0000"></a><div style="min-height:697px" id="datawrapper-vis-45p9T"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/45p9T/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-45p9T"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/45p9T/full.png" alt="Chicago shrank its cultural affairs budget this year, while other big cities raised theirs (Bar Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>In 2026, Chicago allocated about $22.70 per capita to the city’s arts department, trailing behind only New York (which spends $37.72 per capita). But the Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events, known as DCASE, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/city-hall/2025/11/05/chicago-dcase-cultural-affairs-budget-clinee-hedspeth-kenya-merritt-grants-arts" target="_blank" ><u>took a 15% cut</u></a> in the 2026 budget.</p><p>“I think local governments really need to get creative about funding the arts and to really look at new, interesting, dynamic ways to figure out how to increase those resources,” said <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/05/23/erin-harkey-dcase-trump-arts-funding-nea" target="_blank" ><u>Erin Harkey</u></a>, Chicago’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/2024/03/04/chicago-dcase-leadership-in-flux-after-erin-harkey-termination" target="_blank" ><u>former cultural czar</u></a> who now leads the national advocacy group Americans for the Arts.</p><p>And as the city gears up for another <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2026/08/25/mayor-brandon-johnson-refinance-debt-city-hall-budget-deficit" target="_blank" ><u>tough budget fight this fall</u></a>, with some cultural organizations <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/classical-music/2026/05/07/chicago-sinfonietta-layoff-program-pause-finance-classical-music-2027" target="_blank" ><u>gasping for air</u></a> or <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/dance/2025/04/17/chicago-links-hall-dance-closing-small-venue-financial-trouble-arts" target="_blank" ><u>shutting down entirely,</u></a> some arts leaders and advocates worry about what comes next.</p><p>“When the arts and the cultural community contributes to the city in such meaningful and obvious ways, that should also be reflected in the budget,” said Meg Leary, a local artist who recently launched <a class="Link" href="https://www.artsfirstfund.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Arts First</u></a>, a new collective arts fund intended to give dollars directly to artists.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-960000" name="image-960000"></a> The creative sector is actually Chicago’s third-largest industry, accounting for nearly 213,000 jobs, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2026/06/25/creative-economy-impact-study-arts-alliance-illinois-workers" target="_blank" ><u>a 2026 report</u></a> by Arts Alliance Illinois.</p><p>Cultural attractions such as the city’s restaurant scene and outdoor music festivals are <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/mayor/press_room/press_releases/2025/october/summer-tourism-records.html" target="_blank" ><u>tourism generators,</u></a> cites <a class="Link" href="https://www.choosechicago.com/press-media/press-releases/chicago-welcomes-56-8-million-tourists-in-2025-generating-a-record-breaking-21-5-billion-in-spending/" target="_blank" ><u>Choose Chicago</u></a>. The resuscitation of the zombie-like Loop post-COVID? The <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/economy/2025/10/15/chicago-loop-foot-traffic-post-pandemic-arts-culture-events" target="_blank" ><u>arts get much credit</u></a> for that, too.</p><p>Plus, cities with stable support for the arts saw their local creative sectors emerge stronger after the blow dealt by the pandemic, according to <a class="Link" href="https://culturaldata.org/media/3245/cityartssectortrends_fullreport.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>a new national report</u></a> from SMU DataArts in Dallas.</p><p>“Nobody, as an arts worker, is getting up because they’re, like, ‘I’ve got to contribute to the GDP’ or ‘I want to stimulate economic activity on this corridor,’ but these are real facts,” Harkey said. “And if something is this massive and this important to the economy, we have to pay attention to it.”</p><p>Each major city approaches its local arts agency slightly differently: Chicago’s includes the “special events” arm that programs everything from Taste of Chicago to Blues Fest; New York allocates money for city-owned spaces like the Metropolitan Museum of Art; and Houston has a designated external nonprofit partner to distribute grant dollars. In Chicago, DCASE’s funding comes primarily from the city’s special events and hotel tax, plus a mix of public and private grants.</p><p>As New York’s cultural affairs budget increased by 8.1%, local arts funding also climbed in the most recent budget cycles in Phoenix (by 2.3%) and Los Angeles (by 4.7%). In Chicago, funding trended downward in the 2026 budget.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-ff0000" name="html-embed-module-ff0000"></a><div style="min-height:428px" id="datawrapper-vis-GFWHU"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/GFWHU/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-GFWHU"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/GFWHU/full.png" alt="Selected cities’ average spending per resident on cultural affairs departments (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Still, Johnson — who has not confirmed if he will <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/city-hall/2026/08/27/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-august-ask-the-mayor-live-questions-call-phone-number" target="_blank" ><u>seek reelection</u></a> next spring — said he is committed to investing in the sector. In Illinois, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2026/02/23/pritzker-budget-arts-funding-flat-illinois-2026-2027-grants-trump" target="_blank" ><u>funding for the arts</u></a> remained mostly steady under Gov. JB Pritzker’s most recent budget.</p><p>Still, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2025/11/13/nora-daley-richard-m-daley-chicago-arts-culture-architecture-biennial" target="_blank" ><u>Nora Daley</u></a>, board chair of the Illinois Arts Council, said that budget item does not reflect the full picture of what the state spends on the sector.</p><p>“It's a very tough budget time in Illinois, especially with all these federal cuts, so I think we have to look at new models and partnerships,” Daley said.</p><p>When it comes to sourcing further investments in the arts, Johnson pointed again to his trademark theme of progressive revenue — that is, taxing corporations and high-income individuals at a higher level.</p><p>“My preference is always that we're investing more,” Johnson said. “We'll continue to do whatever we can to ensure that the city of Chicago remains at the cutting edge when it comes to not just investments but shaping culture.”</p>

entries.title: Joffrey Ballet President and CEO Greg Cameron to step down in 2027 after helping steer financial turnaround
entries.summary: <p>Joffrey Ballet President and CEO Greg Cameron will step down in December 2027, marking a 15-year tenure that brought more financial stability, the company announced Thursday.</p><p>A board search committee will select a national firm to find Cameron’s replacement, who is expected to start before the end of 2027.</p><p>Cameron, 68, said his succession plan has been in the works for three years, and that he is neither retiring nor moving on to lead another organization. But he plans to stay connected in the Chicago arts community while pursuing other interests.</p><p>“I’m energized,” he told the Sun-Times. “It’s time for me to make room for the next generation of leaders. I've worked in the cultural space in Chicago for 44 years, and over my tenure, I've seen people stay at the party too long. I didn't want to stay at the party too long.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-260000" </figure> </div> </div><p>Since joining the Joffrey in 2013, Cameron has brought financial stability to the organization, eliminating a budget deficit and establishing its first-ever endowment, which has grown to<b> </b>approximately $30 million. During his tenure, the operating budget more than doubled from $13 million to about $33 million.<b> </b>In 2025, the Joffrey <a class="Link" href="https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/364009741" target="_blank" ><u>reported nearly $40 million in revenue</u></a>, making it one of the top-earning arts organizations in the city.</p><p>Cameron is also credited with strengthening Joffrey's international reputation. He oversaw the company’s move from The Auditorium to the Lyric Opera, which has allowed for more ambitious productions, including the critically praised “Frankenstein,” in 2023 and crowdpleaser “Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland” last year. The company opens its 2026-2027 season on Sept. 17 with “Liliom,” which features the choreography of Milwaukee-born dancemaker John Neumeier, the longtime principal choreographer of the Hamburg Ballet.</p><p>Cameron also facilitated partnerships with leading ballet companies on programs, including several with roots in literature, such as “Anna Karenina” with The Australian Ballet, “Princess and the Pea” with Oregon Ballet Theatre, “Atonement” with Ballett Zürich and “Eugene Onegin” with San Francisco Ballet.</p><p>Cameron said the Joffrey was already on a positive artistic trajectory when he started, but he and then-board chair Zachary Lazar determined financial challenges.</p><p>“We had moments of peeling back an onion and discovering, ’This isn't working,’” Cameron said. “We developed specific plans and righted the ship.”</p><p>Part of that strategy was getting the board more engaged in thinking beyond minimum contributions of their “time, talent and treasure,” Cameron said.</p><p>“In my life, success has never been tied to thinking about the minimum,” he said. “If our dancers came into the studio and thought, ‘What's the minimum I can do?,’ we wouldn't be having the success artistically at the box office. it comes to programming, Cameron said he is most proud of growing the “Winning Works” competition, which provides emerging choreographers with opportunities to create new works with dancers from the ballet’s Grainger Academy. Cameron also supported the creation of a documentary about the initiative, “<a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/about/about-pbs/blogs/news/joffrey-ballet-the-next-movement-introduces-five-rising-choreographers-helping-to-redefine-ballet/" target="_blank" ><u>Joffrey Ballet: The Next Movement</u></a>,” directed by Cam Be and produced by Kartemquin Films. It premieres Sept. 18 on PBS.</p><p>Joffrey Artistic Director Ashley Wheater said Cameron’s leadership has allowed him to achieve his creative goals, staging reimagined versions of everything from “The Nutcracker” to “Of Mice and Men.”</p><p>“Greg has really made my dreams become a reality,” Wheater said. “I think it has definitely put the company in a very unique place within America, in that we have a very unique repertoire. You can dream big, but if you can't support those dreams, they're not going to happen.”</p><p>That support included clearing the Joffrey’s debt, unifying the various administration departments and establishing critical partnerships with the Lyric Opera, Chicago Symphony Orchestra and other institutions, Wheater said.</p><p>“He is such a part of the cultural fabric of Chicago,” Wheater said. “And he's charismatic. He knew exactly the right people to talk to in order to get things done. People that had never really been involved with the Joffrey suddenly became very involved. class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cameron strengthened the company’s international reputation by facilitating partnerships with leading ballet companies on programs, including “Eugene Onegin” with San Francisco Ballet this year. Victoria Jaiani, who played the female lead of Tatiana in the production, posed for a portrait in a rehearsal room at the Joffrey Ballet on May 26, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Arthur Maiorella/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Cameron’s other accomplishments include guiding the ballet through the COVID-19 pandemic, establishing the “Joffrey for All” commitment to accessibility and expanding dance education in Chicago Public Schools. He also supported ongoing union efforts, negotiating two five-year contracts with the American Guild of Musical Artists. He said he hopes to solidify a third five-year agreement this fall.</p><p>Under his leadership, the Joffrey has also partnered with other cultural institutions on a plan to revitalize Downtown with a so-called “<a class="Link" href="https://www.culturalstadium.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Cultural Stadium</u></a>” concept that would pair events and architectural features. Among those projects is Poetry Way, an activation of the alley between Joffrey Tower and the Chicago Theatre, which will launch on Oct. 17 during the Chicago Loop Alliance Arts Fest.</p><p>“I am part of a team that has accomplished all of this,” he said of his overall success at the Joffrey. “I am not the artistic director. I can't dance. I don't sing. I don't paint. I don't draw.”</p><p>Despite that, Cameron has had a passion for the arts since he was a child in Westchester. He even created a makeshift museum in his basement, charging neighborhood kids to see his grandparents’ tchotchkes from their travels around the world, as well as his pet boa constrictor. Then, he graduated to hosting theater productions<b>.</b></p><p>“I was not performing,” he said. “I was printing the tickets, advertising and closing the garage door between acts.”</p><div partnerships with the Lyric Opera, Chicago Symphony Orchestra and other institutions.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Cameron went on to earn a bachelor’s degree in German from Illinois State University and a master’s degree in public administration from the University of Illinois. He interned for the Chicago Department of Cultural Affairs and built a career in arts administration and philanthropy, holding positions at the Museum Of Contemporary Art Chicago, Art Institute of Chicago and WTTW/WFMT.</p><p>Cameron said he is looking forward to spending more time with his partner and family, and may consider writing or teaching. As for the next chapter of the Joffrey, he said the organization is on solid footing, even as the arts industry faces funding deficits and rising costs, and is forced to contend with unpredictable audience attendance..</p><p>There are ample opportunities to grow the company, whether it's adding more dancers, expanding the footprint of Grainger Academy or exploring more community partnerships, he said.</p><p>“We got so much more done than I ever dreamt I was going to be able to do,” he said. “It’s hard to leave when you love what you're doing. But it’s better to leave when you're at the top of your game.”</p>

entries.title: Are cicadas louder this year?
entries.summary: <p>From Garfield Park to Lake View, from Oak Park to Belmont-Cragin, cicadas are singing their summer chorus across the Chicago area.</p><h3>Cicadas make a racket every summer. But is the cacophony of buzzing, whirring and droning louder this year?</h3><p>It’s “inconclusive” whether they’re louder, said Spencer Campbell, the Morton Arboretum's senior manager of natural areas. Anecdotally, Campbell said, cicadas seem louder this year, which could have something to do with a very hot summer in the Chicago area. But some studies have shown that cicadas are actually less active in warm weather, he noted.</p><p>People may be more attuned to the insects because in 2024, Illinois was the epicenter of a once-in-a-lifetime <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cicadas" ><u>convergence of cicadas</u></a> that emerge every 13 and 17 years.</p><p>There may also be more of them than usual. Nina Salem, founder of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/06/05/insect-asylum-aims-to-inspire-with-public-cicada-art-now-on-display-cicada-parade-a" >Insect Asylum</a> in Avondale, has noticed more cicadas compared with last year.<b></b></p><p>Two weeks ago in Palmer Square, cicada nymphs were crawling out of the ground and climbing onto Salem like a tree. “I can’t remember the last time in the city that cicadas were emerging underneath me and crawling up,” she said.</p><p>“We definitely have more luck in finding them than before,” said Salem, who opened the Insect Asylum’s museum in 2022. “We’ve had a really cool cicada season.”</p><p>Cicadas do seem louder this year, observed Salem, though she noted that’s based on her personal experience, not science.</p><p>She wondered if more-forested areas like Thatcher Woods, LaBagh Woods and Skokie Lagoons are seeing — and hearing — more cicadas.</p><h3>Why do cicadas buzz so loudly?</h3><p>Males are sounding off ardent mating calls to attract females. They can climb high into trees “trying to yell louder than their neighbor,” said Campbell. Cicada choruses can exceed nine decibels — a noise level similar to that of lawnmowers, motorcycles and tractors. “Areas with more mature trees could have a louder chorus,” he said.</p><h3>What kind of cicadas are these?</h3><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/cicada-watch-2024/2024/05/24/periodical-cicadas-sound-buzzing-chicago-illinois" ><u>trademark end-of-summer buzzing</u></a> is coming from “dog-day” cicadas. They are annual cicadas, which is a misnomer since they can emerge every year or every two to five years, said Campbell. They come out only for a few weeks in the summer to mate before dying off. Their peak time is now. “A month from now this will be a distant memory,” he said.</p><p>Annual cicadas usually sing at dusk. Periodical cicadas that emerge every few years or more are loudest in the late morning and early afternoon.</p><h3>Are these cicadas part of the 2024 convergence?</h3><p>No. In 2024, for the first time in more than 200 years, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/outdoors/2024/03/14/cicadas-2024-illinois-map-schedule" >two types of periodical cicadas came above ground at the same time</a>. One brood, or breeding group, emerges every 13 years, and the other comes every 17 years.</p><p>In 1803, the last time that natural phenomenon took place, “electricity hadn’t been invented, horses and carriages were still the main way to get around, and the Great Chicago Fire hadn’t yet ravaged the city,” wrote Sun-Times reporter <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/mary-norkol" ><u>Mary Norkol</u></a> in 2024. Norkol has written extensively about cicadas.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-190000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A periodical cicada flies away from Stephanie Adams, plant healthcare leader at the Morton Arboretum, Friday, May 17, 2024. The periodical cicadas have emerged in the Chicago area for the first time in 17 years.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Scientists and researchers, like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/outdoors/2024/03/14/cicadas-2024-illinois-map-schedule" target="_blank" ><u>Kacie Athey</u></a> of the University of Illinois, encouraged people to appreciate that rare occurrence.</p><p>“We talk about this as being a once-in-a-lifetime thing where two are coming out at once, it’s more than that. … The next time we can expect to see two broods to come up is 2245,” Athey said then.</p><p>When the cicadas emerged from their years feeding underground, one <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/6/3/23747337/chicago-outdoors-here-come-the-cicadas" ><u>brood that emerges every 17 years</u></a> was centered in northern Illinois, while the 13-year brood was found in the southern part of the state.</p><p>Although the 2024 event captured headlines, this year’s annual emergence is “exciting,” said Salem of the Insect Asylum. She noted that the general public doesn’t celebrate more common events as much.</p><h3>How are people coping with cicada noise?</h3><p>Even if this year’s cicada ruckus is at normal levels, some people on social media describe their droning as “deafening.”</p><p>At Keshet, a private therapeutic day school in Northbrook, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/cicada-watch-2024/2024/05/06/cicadas-autism-sensory-sensibilities" >students with disabilities and sensory sensitivities again prepared for cicada noise</a> and changes in their environment.</p><p>“Many of Keshet’s programs are located in Chicago’s northern suburbs, and the cicadas have been really, really loud this summer,” Jennifer Phillips, president and CEO of Keshet, said in an email. “Our staff continue to be aware of how the noise can affect individuals differently and provide support and accommodations as needed.”</p><p>Students, ranging in age from 12 to 15, go over <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2017/12/6/18375402/blue-mind-why-being-near-the-water-makes-you-happy" ><u>coping mechanisms</u></a> if the cicada noise becomes overwhelming, such as going inside to take breaks from the noise, putting on headphones or chewing on a toy to help distract themselves.</p>
